evidence_quotes.quote: For the residential customer class in the municipally-owned water industry, the useable formula for the welfare loss triangle depends on the divergence between price and long run marginal cost and the price elasticity of demand.
Under the assumption of constant costs in the range of output levels produced by firms of medium size, the deadweight welfare loss triangle ABC is depicted in Figure 1.

ESTIMATION OF MONOPOLY WELFARE LOSS is expressed as a percentage of the residential consumer's annual water bill. The data were selected from the same 1965 American Water Works Association survey used in the estimation of the cost functions.

Although prices are in excess of marginal cost for utilities facing both state regulation and local regulation, there are statistically discernible differences in welfare losses between the two groups (see Table 2). In those states that regulate the rate structures of municipally owned utilities as well as private utilities, the average welfare loss was 4.6 per cent lower in Model 1 and 4.24 per cent lower in Model 2.

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. Instead, it is an industrial-organization microeconomic study measuring Harberger deadweight allocative welfare loss from pricing above long-run marginal cost for existing residential customer classes of U.S. municipally owned water utilities.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines a regulatory factor, comparing state public utility commission regulation versus local municipal regulation (by city councils or water commissions) of municipally owned water utility rate structures. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — regulatory jurisdiction over rate structures is analysed solely in relation to allocative deadweight loss (price-marginal cost markup) across aggregate utility residential revenues rather than as a rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 are not satisfied.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical analysis of cross-sectional utility operating data from the 1965 (and 1960) American Water Works Association surveys, using OLS regressions to estimate long-run marginal cost (n = 95 and n = 87 utilities) and comparing deadweight welfare loss across 88 locally regulated and 27 state-regulated utilities.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports only imputed Harberger deadweight welfare loss (allocative inefficiency triangle derived from price-marginal cost divergence and regional price elasticity parameters) as a percentage of residential annual water revenue. Does not report outcomes measuring service access, connection, availability, reliability, actual water quantity consumed across regulatory regimes, household affordability/burden (explicitly noting the low cost of water), or exclusion/disconnection.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (U.S. municipally owned water utilities' residential customer class; n = 115 utilities in welfare-loss comparison), exposure (state PUC rate regulation vs. local council/commission regulation), outcome (deadweight monopoly welfare loss as percent of residential revenue), and cross-sectional econometric design are all clearly identifiable.

population_and_sample: U.S. municipally-owned water utilities (residential customer class) from the 1965 and 1960 American Water Works Association Surveys of Operating Data (n = 95 for variable cost/distribution loss regressions; n = 87 for fixed cost regression; n = 88 locally regulated and n = 27 state-regulated utilities in the welfare-loss comparison)
exposure: State-level public utility commission regulation of municipally-owned water utility rate structures (five states) versus local regulation by city councils or water commissions
outcome: Imputed Harberger deadweight monopoly welfare loss (based on divergence between average residential price and estimated long-run marginal cost and regional price elasticities) as a percentage of the residential customer class's annual water bill/revenue
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails c1 and narrow c2). Bruggink (1985) is an empirical public-utility economics study comparing state public utility commission regulation (n = 27) and local municipal regulation (n = 88) of U.S. municipal water utilities, but its sole outcome is the imputed Harberger deadweight allocative welfare loss triangle (divergence between price and long-run marginal cost combined with externally estimated regional price elasticities) expressed as a share of residential utility revenue. It does not examine water service access (c1 = no) and reports no outcome measuring access, connection, availability, reliability, observed consumption quantity differences, household affordability, or exclusion (c4 = no). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 it examines regulatory structure, whereas under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading regulatory structure is not examined as a mechanism governing service access; under both readings the study is excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 fail.
